1: The AI Jobpocalypse isn't panning out as experts have predicted
2: "People should stop training radiologists now...it's just completely obvious that within 5 years Deep Learning is going to do better than radiologists...it might be 10 years, but we've got plenty of radiologists already"
Dr. Geoffrey Hinton, Deep Learning pioneer and winner of the 2024 Nobel Prize in physics
3: Since 2016, the number of radiologists billing medicare has grown at almost 2x the rate of all doctors.
4: CAPABILITY: 76% of FDA-cleared AI tools are for radiology. But a full AI takeover has been much slower than he predicted. In 2023, Hinton himself admitted to being off by a factor of three. Instead of 5 years, it would probably take 15.
5: It's a case of Amara's Law: "We tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate the effect in the long run."
Hinton might yet be right about his prediction...
6: PRESCRIPTION: "People should stop training radiologists now"
It seems Dr. Hinton was guilty of "epistemic trespassing," where an expert in one field makes judgments in fields where he has no expertise.
7: Evaluating scans is NOT all a radiologist does. A small 2012 Canadian study estimated that it only takes up about 36% of their time. The rest includes performing hands-on procedures and supervising and monitoring.
8: Imaging has become a bigger part of treatment in general. And the population over 65--the people in most need of scans--has risen 24% since 2016. Meanwhile, the number of radiologists hasn't kept pace.
9: If AI were replacing radiologists, they'd get cheaper relative to other doctors, but the opposite happened. Rather than being automated, radiologists are in more demand than they were 10 years ago.
